props.title: Lola
props.initialSlug: A cabaret singer dreams of stardom in 1950s Germany

sections.content: Rainer Werner Fassbinder's Lola (1981) stands as a dazzling critique of post-war German society, completing his BRD (Bundesrepublik Deutschland) trilogy alongside The Marriage of Maria Braun (1979) and Veronika Voss (1982). Set in the economic miracle years of the 1950s, Fassbinder uses oversaturated colors and melodramatic flourishes to expose corruption beneath Germany's reconstruction. Barbara Sukowa delivers a powerhouse performance as Lola, a cabaret singer/prostitute who manipulates local officials - a direct homage to Marlene Dietrich's character in The Blue Angel (1930).

sections.content: The film's visual style deliberately echoes Douglas Sirk's 1950s melodramas like All That Heaven Allows (1955), but Fassbinder pushes the artificiality to extremes. His signature use of mirrors, frames-within-frames, and lurid lighting creates a heightened reality that underscores the moral decay. The brothel scenes glow with unnatural pinks and blues, while the government offices maintain a sterile fluorescent pallor - visually connecting capitalism and corruption.

Lola forms a spiritual connection with later films examining post-war German society, particularly The Tin Drum (1979) and Wings of Desire (1987). Like those works, it uses heightened reality and symbolic characters to process national trauma. The film's influence extends to modern German cinema, seen in works like Phoenix (2014) and Barbara (2012) which similarly explore moral compromise in periods of social upheaval. sections.content: Within Fassbinder's prolific career (he made over 40 features before his death at 37), the BRD trilogy represents his most focused examination of German society. Lola specifically targets the "economic miracle" of the 1950s, using its prostitute protagonist as a metaphor for a country selling its soul for prosperity. This theme resonates with later German films like The Lives of Others (2006) and Downfall (2004), which similarly excavate difficult periods in national history.
